cards.headline: Alberta government asks judge to dismiss First Nation's challenge of sovereignty act

pages.text: The Alberta government is asking a judge to strike down a constitutional challenge brought by the Onion Lake Cree Nation regarding the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act. Lawyers argued in an Edmonton court for the government's application to stop the claim from proceeding to trial, with the province arguing that the First Nation has not shown the act has had any impact on treaty rights. Court of King's Bench Justice Grant Dunlop has reserved his decision on the matter. The Onion Lake Cree Nation, which straddles the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary, argues the act is unconstitutional because it conflicts with the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown and has asked the court to declare the law unenforceable. Chief Pete Chief told reporters outside the court that the law was passed without meaningful consultation and raises questions about treaty rights and the limits of provincial authority, stating that treaty rights existed before Alberta was created and did not disappear when the province was established.

The Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was the flagship first law of Premier Danielle Smith, who used it as a signature proposal during her 2022 leadership win of the United Conservative Party. Smith stated the act was necessary to resist federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction. When Smith first invoked the law, she conceded that it was symbolic and that she did not need it to implement new measures to oppose federal energy regulations. The province maintains that the act does not authorize anything that would contravene federal law or the Canadian Constitution.

cards.headline: Bank of England chief economist signals likely interest rate rises to combat inflation

pages.text: Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill has stated that the central bank will probably need to raise interest rates again, potentially in early 2027, to combat rising inflation. This follows a recent decision to increase interest rates from 3.75% to 4%. Pill told the Financial Times that while the recent increase was a “significant step” toward improving monetary policy, “we have further to go.” The move signals a potential rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who must refinance their loans. Pill indicated he is poised to vote for another quarter-point increase, noting his view that the central bank “waited too long” to act against inflation.

Inflation is expected to rise to 5% in spring, driven by high oil and gas prices resulting from the Iran war. Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which he believes could keep inflation high for a longer period. He expressed concern that the inflationary impact could be magnified by “second-round effects,” where wage increases lead to further price hikes. Pill told the Financial Times that he considers an end to the US-Israeli conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability.” While the Bank has not yet seen evidence of companies passing higher costs to consumers or significant wage increases, Pill stated that “the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.” Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027.

cards.headline: Investigators in Hungary find $19.5m in hidden cash during corruption probe

pages.text: Hungarian investigators seized $19.5m in cash, including bundles buried in forests, during searches conducted on November 12 and 13, 2026. The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), a new agency established to investigate the suspected misuse of public money, reported that the money was found in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary. The recovered funds consisted of 5,071,632,000 Hungarian forints, €2,658,350, and US $1,257,100. Investigators located the cash in farm buildings, warehouses, a home, a high-value safe in a secluded location, and beneath the ground in forests. Finance Minister Andras Karman stated on Facebook on November 13, 2026, that 12 treasury employees spent eight hours counting the money. The cash was subsequently deposited with the state treasury. This discovery is part of an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, who served as Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018. Sesztak is suspected of receiving more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks related to government construction projects and the purchase of overpriced secondhand buses by a state transport company. He was detained in September and denies any wrongdoing.

cards.headline: Turkey's approval of Makkah Defence Pact takes effect following separate agreement with Qatar

pages.text: Turkey's law approving the Makkah Defence Pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan has taken effect following its publication in the country's official gazette. This legislative step follows the Turkish parliament's ratification of the agreement on November 5, which passed with 279 votes to 119. The Makkah Defence Pact, signed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan in August, is modeled after NATO's Article 5, meaning an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The pact aims to strengthen intelligence sharing, military co-ordination, and defence industry co-operation among the three nations. The implementation of the pact comes as Saudi Arabia faces intensified attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis, including strikes on airports and claims of attacks on energy and military targets. Despite the collective defence commitment provided by Turkey, which hosts NATO's second-largest army, Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler has ruled out deploying troops to fight the Houthis under the agreement.

The activation of the Makkah Defence Pact follows a separate mutual defence agreement signed between Turkey and Qatar on November 13, 2026. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met in Istanbul to co-chair the Supreme Strategic Committee, resulting in a range of bilateral agreements. According to a joint statement, the mutual defence agreement between Ankara and Doha is aimed at bolstering collective defence and achieving regional security and stability. The agreement seeks to establish a unified position for both parties in the event of an external armed attack targeting either or both nations.

cards.headline: Hundreds of children in England prescribed GLP-1 weight-loss medications

pages.text: An investigation by The Guardian has found that hundreds of children in England have been prescribed GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12 years old. GLP-1 medications, such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, were originally developed to help people with type 2 diabetes manage blood sugar levels but have become widely used as slimming aids. Data obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests shows that in the 2025-26 financial year, 419 prescriptions were issued to children under the age of 18, with 10 of those issued to children under the age of 12. These figures relate to prescriptions in England that were dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK. The total number of children receiving these medications is likely a considerable underestimate, as the data does not include prescriptions dispensed in hospitals, in prisons, or via private prescriptions. One private clinic for children has previously reported having more than 200 patients receiving the injections.

In the four-month period from April to July, 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to children, 15 of whom were under the age of 12. It remains unclear whether the recorded figures reflect medications being used primarily for weight loss. Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, stated that while the number of prescriptions is small compared to the scale of childhood obesity, those using the drugs require long-term lifestyle changes.

cards.headline: New U.S. national policy for organ retrieval procedure sparks ethical debate

pages.text: The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The procedure, called normothermic regional perfusion (NRP), involves doctors attaching an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they have been declared dead. This pump restores blood flow to the donor's heart, lungs, kidneys, liver, and other organs to prevent them from deteriorating. Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration—the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system—stated that the hope for NRP is that it increases both the supply and the quality of organs, which could help solve the chronic organ shortage.

While the new guidelines are designed to protect potential donors during the retrieval procedure, bioethicists have raised troubling questions. The procedure can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there is no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. Critics argue that the guidelines do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns regarding the process.

cards.headline: Survivors recount terror following deadly Brooklyn building collapse

pages.text: Survivors of a three-story apartment building collapse in Brooklyn, New York, recounted their grief and terror during a news conference. The collapse killed eight people, including two children aged 9 and 10, according to city officials. At least 18 people were injured in the incident, including four firefighters. New York officials, including building inspectors and prosecutors, are investigating why the building fell while workers were digging at an adjacent construction site. Those who lost neighbors, family, and homes demanded answers during the briefing.

Mamadou Mouctar Balde reported that he had stepped out to buy groceries when the collapse occurred, leaving his pregnant wife and two roommates, 31-year-old Mamadou N’Diaye and 23-year-old Mamadou Barry, at home. While Balde's pregnant wife was pulled alive from the rubble, his two roommates perished. Balde stated that Barry was cooking and N’Diaye was sleeping on the couch at the time; upon returning, Balde initially assumed a traffic accident had occurred after seeing police, firefighters, and neighbors gathered outside. Ciahola Lawrence, a resident of the building next to the collapsed structure, described waking from a nap to find her bedroom wall gone, exposing an abyss of dust and debris. Lawrence, who was evacuated from the building, said she saw neighbors being carried out on stretchers and stated, “We didn’t deserve this.”

cards.headline: Rescue of 56 people from Teknaf trafficking network exposes criminal activity in Cox’s Bazar

pages.text: The rescue of 56 people from a human trafficking network in the hills of Teknaf has revealed the scale of organized criminal activity along the Cox’s Bazar border. According to The Daily Star, the victims were mostly Bangladeshis held captive by armed traffickers. These traffickers reportedly demanded exorbitant sums for the victims' release or for illegal sea passage to Malaysia. Some victims were lured with promises of employment before being sold to the traffickers. A survivor reported that workers seeking honest living were abducted, blindfolded, beaten, and kept in remote hideouts, with demands for freedom reaching up to Tk 4 lakh.

The danger posed by these networks was demonstrated during a rescue operation on November 5, which resulted in the killing of an army soldier. Reports indicate that some of the armed guards involved in the trafficking were children, and police have named a 15-year-old among the accused. The Daily Star notes that the ability of these operations to continue in an area with a substantial presence of security forces and law enforcement raises questions about the criminal ecosystem. Additionally, the vast Rohingya refugee population in Cox’s Bazar remains vulnerable to traffickers' false promises regarding employment, marriage, or family reunification abroad due to restricted livelihoods and declining assistance.

cards.headline: Three people dead after boat crashes into unknown object on Squamish River in B.C.

pages.text: Three people are dead and several others were rescued after a boat crashed into an unknown object on the Squamish River in British Columbia during stormy conditions. The Sea-to-Sky RCMP confirmed the third fatality after locating the body of a person who had been listed as missing. While the identities of the deceased have not been confirmed, police stated that two of the victims were female and one was male. Robert Dykstra of the Sea-to-Sky RCMP said there were approximately eight people on the boat when the accident occurred. The RCMP responded to the incident at 1:52 p.m.

The crash occurred amid significant rainfall over a 48-hour period and substantial flooding. According to Dykstra, the boat ran into an object, causing it to stop and throwing people into the water. While a number of people were rescued, they were located on the opposite side of the Squamish River in an area without direct road access. Ashley MacKay noted that the conditions were extremely difficult and unsafe for emergency responders. Investigators are working to determine the owner of the boat and why it was on the river during the harsh weather. Squamish Valley Road, which provides vehicle access to the remote area, is currently closed at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge due to flooding, and the road was washed out approximately two or three kilometres north of the Cheekye area.

cards.headline: Syria reverses visa preapproval requirement for US and UK citizens

pages.text: Syria has canceled a requirement for citizens of the United States and the United Kingdom to obtain prior approval before entering the country, restoring previous entry procedures. The reversal follows backlash from observers on social media who warned the restrictions could undermine efforts to revive Syria's tourism sector. On November 12, 2026, Mazen Alloush, the director of international relations at Syria’s General Authority for Ports and Customs, told the fact-checking platform Taakkad that entry procedures for US citizens have returned to normal. Alloush stated the requirement to obtain approval before entering Syria had been imposed “temporarily” by the Interior Ministry. Syrian Assistant Foreign Minister for Consular Affairs Mohammed Yaqoub al-Omar also confirmed to the SANA news outlet that the requirement for US and UK citizens to obtain prior approval had been canceled, noting it had been implemented temporarily. Previously, US citizens had been added to a list requiring preapproval alongside Egyptian, Tunisian, and some East Asian nationals. While the restriction was in place, some US citizens reported on social media that they had been turned away because they lacked advance visas. According to Alloush, citizens from the Gulf and Europe could continue to obtain tourist visas on arrival.

cards.headline: Man pronounced dead following early morning stabbing in Mississauga

pages.text: A man is dead following a stabbing in Mississauga. Peel Region police responded to reports of a stabbing inside a building at Lakeshore Road East and Fergus Avenue, just west of Dixie Road, around 4:45 a.m. Officers arriving at the scene found a man with life-threatening injuries and obvious signs of trauma; he was pronounced dead at the scene. The age of the victim was not immediately known. A resident of the building told CityNews that a large police presence was observed around a first-floor unit.

Amanda Steenson stated that it is unclear if police are searching for one or more suspects, and no immediate description of a suspect was available. While Steenson said the stabbing appears to be an isolated incident, it remains uncertain if the victim and a suspect were known to each other.

cards.headline: Arbitrator imposes first union contract for Amazon workers in North America

pages.text: An independent arbitrator has imposed a three-year binding collective agreement for approximately 800 Amazon workers in Delta, British Columbia, marking the first such contract for the company's workers in North America. Both the union Unifor and Amazon confirmed the terms were set by an arbitrator rather than through direct negotiation between the parties. In August, the British Columbia Labour Relations Board ruled in favor of using binding arbitration to settle the labor dispute, a process the e-commerce company fought against.

Unifor national president Lana Payne praised the workers for their courage, stating they proved the company wrong after Amazon suggested a union contract would never happen. Payne alleged that Amazon used its power and money to deter workers and tried to convince them they were too large to organize. According to Unifor, the new agreement includes wage increases that will bring hourly rates to $29 by the end of the contract, enhanced severance protections, and an additional week of vacation for employees with 10 years of service.

Amazon has criticized the process, with vice-president J. Ofori Agboka stating in an online posting that the imposition was improper, unfair, and defies common sense. Agboka noted that workers were not allowed to vote on the agreement and said the company would take its concerns to court if necessary. He also expressed concern that union dues could result in workers taking home less money than they did previously.

cards.headline: Houthis threaten Sanaa private schools with fines and closure over military mobilization rallies

pages.text: The Houthi-led education ministry in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, is threatening dozens of private schools with fines and closure for refusing to participate in military mobilization activities. According to school sources told Asharq Al-Awsat, the militia has ordered private schools in Sanaa and its outskirts to hold at least three student marches and rallies per week. These events, held both on school grounds and in nearby streets, are intended to promote the militia's military escalation in Taiz and other battlefronts and to glorify its leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi. School administrators in the Safiya, Sabeen, Azal, Wehda, and Tahrir districts have resisted these orders, citing pressure from parents who are threatening to withdraw their children due to disrupted lessons and activities unrelated to education.

The mobilization efforts coincide with a military escalation in several provinces in recent weeks and follow accusations that the militia is seeking to recruit more fighters from among students. Since seizing control of Sanaa, the Houthis have revised school curricula and introduced sectarian and mobilization activities, which has drawn warnings from the United Nations and human rights groups regarding the ideological indoctrination and military recruitment of children. The Houthis have reportedly used annual school license renewals as a pressure tactic to force administrators to comply with the mobilization orders. Education professionals told Asharq Al-Awsat they are increasingly alarmed by these events, noting that students are being forced to participate daily. In the Azal district, a teacher reported that the rallies are taking time away from core subjects and cutting into school schedules.

Local families have expressed significant concern regarding the impact of these activities on their children's education and safety. One parent in Sanaa, speaking on condition of anonymity, stated that after school administrations informed families that children were required to attend the rallies, they feared the militia might eventually send children to the frontlines. The parent also noted the financial strain of tuition and transportation, stating, 'now they want to turn our children into tools for their activities.' Educators and community members have characterized the measures as a violation of children's right to education and a threat to their future.

cards.headline: US officials and experts call for crackdown on illegal mining as 60% of Ghana's freshwater sources face degradation

pages.text: United States officials and scientific experts are calling for an urgent crackdown on galamsey—illegal small-scale gold mining—to address mercury pollution that has degraded an estimated 60 per cent of Ghana’s freshwater sources. During a symposium in Accra on November 10, 2026, experts warned that the pollution threatens public health, food security, and economic opportunity by contaminating rivers, fish, farm products, and drinking water. The symposium, titled “Addressing Mercury Pollution: Collaborative Solutions for Sustainable Mining in Ghana,” was organized by the U.S. Embassy on behalf of the Regional Environment, Science, Technology, and Health Hub for West and Central Africa to unite various sectors in reducing mercury use and promoting sustainable mining practices.

The environmental impact of mercury use in mining is documented through several specific findings. A 2024 baseline assessment by the US Geological Survey in Ghana's Western Region found that total mercury in unfiltered water from the Ankobra and Pra rivers was more than 55 times higher than the US average, while river sediments were two to 25 times higher. Additionally, turbidity—a measure of water cloudiness—in the Birim River reportedly reached 63 million Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), significantly exceeding the maximum treatable level of 200 NTU and rendering a community water treatment plant unable to function. Sarah Cobb of the US Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs (OES) noted that the scale of destruction is largely attributed to illegal small-scale mining and the indiscriminate use of mercury to extract gold.

Health experts highlighted that mercury pollution poses severe risks to human biology, including potential harm to developing brains, heart tissue, and reproductive health for pregnant mothers and their babies. To combat these issues, Sarah Cobb cited existing Ghanaian initiatives, such as a five-step anti-galamsey plan and a drone-equipped command centre operated by the Minerals Commission. Cobb urged the government to enforce the law and fund restoration, the industry to adopt clean technologies, and scientists to use data to inform decisions, while calling for sustained support from development partners.

cards.headline: Gadi Eisenkot condemns Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens

pages.text:
Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot condemned a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens on November 13, 2026. Eisenkot, a prominent Jewish political leader, stated that Arab citizens are “an integral part of the Israeli story” and characterized attempts to marginalize and vilify them collectively as a “profound violation of the principles of statesmanship.”

The condemnation follows accusations by caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Arab parties engaged in electoral fraud. Netanyahu has repeatedly targeted Palestinian citizens of Israel and Arab parties, accusing them of manipulating the election and having links to Hamas. However, Israeli electoral authorities have rejected these claims, stating they are not backed by evidence.

The political tension follows the October election, in which the two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured 19 seats. These parties hold significant influence as potential kingmakers in the formation of a new government.

The controversy also involves Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security branch, which sought to question four Arab lawmakers, including Mansour Abbas, the head of the Arab-majority Ra’am party. This move led to accusations that the security agency has become politicised.

Arab citizens of Israel, the vast majority of whom are of Palestinian descent, comprise more than 20% of the country’s population. Eisenkot currently faces the task of balancing the interests of several parties to form a coalition. If he cannot form a government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, the mandate to form a government may pass to another lawmaker, such as Netanyahu.

cards.headline: Bank of Ghana attributes GH¢50 portrait resemblance to technical design adjustments

pages.text: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has attributed the altered appearance of Theodosia Salome Okoh on the new GH¢50 Heritage Series banknote to technical and security adjustments made during the design process. In a press release issued by its Communications Department on November 13, 2026, the central bank confirmed the portrait was developed from multiple photographs of Mrs. Okoh, the designer of Ghana's national flag, and not from an image of her sister, Dr. Letitia Obeng. The bank explained that the selected photographs were used to create an engraved artistic representation suitable for banknote printing, but modifications were necessary to satisfy strict technical and security requirements for currency production. These adaptations, including replacing Mrs. Okoh's signature head-tie with a hairstyle common to her era, contributed to the perceived differences in her appearance and resulted in an image bearing a close likeness to Dr. Obeng.

The clarification follows public discourse sparked by a social media post from Dr. Eddie Obeng, the son of Dr. Letitia Obeng and nephew of Theodosia Okoh. Dr. Obeng expressed astonishment that his mother's likeness appeared on the note instead of his aunt's, stating the resemblance was unmistakable. This prompted widespread discussion among Ghanaians regarding the error on a national currency. To address the controversy, BoG board member Beatrice Feehi Annangfio issued a statement on Facebook explaining the design process. The bank reaffirmed that the portrait is intended to honor Mrs. Okoh and her contribution to Ghana's national identity, stating it is committed to representing distinguished personalities on the country's currency with dignity and respect.

cards.headline: Canada appoints Dorothy Myo as Commissioner of Indigenous Languages

pages.text: Canada has appointed Dorothy Myo as the new Commissioner of Indigenous Languages. Myo takes over the role as the office faces questions regarding its financial management and operations. She replaces interim commissioner Candice St-Aubin, who issued a statement congratulating Myo on November 10, 2026. St-Aubin stated that Myo's leadership and experience would help guide the commission during an urgent period for Indigenous language revitalization efforts. The commissioner is appointed to a five-year term by the Governor in Council, following a recommendation from the minister of Canadian Heritage and consultations with Indigenous leadership and communities.

The position of Indigenous languages commissioner was created to fulfill Call to Action 15 from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. This specific mandate urged the federal government to appoint a commissioner to promote Indigenous languages and evaluate whether federal funding for language initiatives is adequate. The role follows the 2019 passage of the Indigenous Languages Act. Ronald E. Ignace served as Canada's first Commissioner of Indigenous Languages after being appointed in 2021. Myo, who was raised on Saulteaux First Nation in Saskatchewan and speaks Cree and Saulteaux, previously held senior roles with various federal and provincial Indigenous organizations, including serving as head of the Saskatchewan Indigenous Cultural Centre.

cards.headline: Ghana Police begin installing speed camera warning signs following Mahama directive

pages.text: The Ghana Police Service and road safety agencies have started installing large advance warning signboards along key road corridors to alert motorists to automated TraffiTech-GH speed cameras. This rollout follows a directive from President John Dramani Mahama, who called for administrative transparency by ensuring drivers receive clear prior notice of camera locations. The initiative addresses criticisms from private motorists and commercial transport operators who argued that enforcing automated fines without visible warnings amounted to entrapment after the TraffiTech-GH system launched on November 1, 2026. TraffiTech-GH is an automated traffic enforcement system operated by the Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) of the Ghana Police Service that uses fixed, mobile, and radar camera sensors to capture speeding violations in real time.

During the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, President Mahama supported the technology as a tool to reduce pedestrian fatalities but emphasized the need for visible notices. He stated that the police and those implementing TraffiTech should put up signposts warning motorists of upcoming cameras to maintain transparency. Recent photographs of the installation process show police personnel and technical crews using heavy lifting machinery to mount large blue-and-yellow reflective gantries. Some of the new billboards feature a camera icon alongside a red-ringed 80 km/h speed limit sign, while others include inscriptions such as “24-hrs speed camera monitoring” and “Speed kills, kill it now.” One sign captured in photographs shows a 50 m speed limit sign near ACP Alexander Kwaku Obeng, the Director of Education, Research and Training at the MTTD.

cards.headline: Bangladeshi photographer Pinu Rahman wins USD 200,000 prize for photograph of fire victims

pages.text: Bangladeshi photographer Pinu Rahman has won the grand prize at the Hamdan International Photography Award (HIPA), an award based in the United Arab Emirates, for a photograph depicting a family sleeping in a room gutted by fire. The prize includes USD 200,000, which is nearly Tk 25 million. The photograph captures a humanitarian message of a family's unbroken bond and love for one another despite losing everything in the blaze. Rahman shared the details of the photograph's origin with Prothom Alo's Sozib Mia.

The photograph depicts the aftermath of a fire that broke out at the Korail slum in Dhaka on 25 November 2025. Rahman, who works as a banker, stated he could not visit the scene on the day of the fire because he had to go to the office. He decided to photograph the aftermath of the incident, a practice he has followed in similar past events. On 13 November 2026, Rahman reached the scene at approximately 5:30 or 6:00 am to take photographs.

cards.headline: Sentencing delayed for Edmonton man who left beaten girlfriend to drown

pages.text: Sentencing has been delayed for Collin Boucher-Gionet in the Court of King’s Bench of Alberta following his conviction for the 2024 death of Aylissa Rovere. The prosecution and defence are currently debating how Boucher-Gionet should be held culpable for the killing. 36-year-old Boucher-Gionet pleaded guilty to manslaughter and attempting to improperly interfere with or offer indignity to human remains. He was initially charged with second-degree murder but pleaded to the reduced manslaughter charge in 2025. An agreed statement of facts revealed that Boucher-Gionet prepared to burn and then bury Rovere before disposing of her inside a septic tank in 2024, believing she was already dead. However, an autopsy showed Rovere was still alive and died of drowning hours later.

Rovere, a 32-year-old mother of two, was last seen alive in September. Her body was discovered the following week during a police search of a home in Parkland County, located approximately 40 kilometres west of downtown Edmonton. Crown prosecutor Anders Quist told the court that the pair had shared a long relationship marked by domestic violence. On the night she was last seen, the pair had met on the rural Parkland County property to share a firepit with friends; witnesses described them as “lovey-dovey” at the time. While the circumstances of her death were horrific, Rovere's family has expressed a desire for her to be remembered beyond the violence of her passing.

cards.headline: Report finds Canadian students still recovering from pandemic-related learning loss

pages.text: Canadian students continue to face declining academic achievement, particularly in mathematics, as they recover from pandemic-era school disruptions, according to a report released by the Royal Society of Canada, the Canadian Commission for UNESCO, and the University of Ottawa. The report examined academic results in language arts and mathematics before, during, and after COVID-19 to analyze learning loss and recovery efforts across the country. Tracy Vaillancourt, the report's chair and a professor of education at the University of Ottawa, stated that the pandemic's influence on learning is expected to be felt for generations to come. The findings showed that results varied by region, grade, and student population, which Vaillancourt attributed to different local contexts, such as how jurisdictions assessed learning and the varying approaches taken to school closures, remote learning, and classroom physical distancing.

Nearly three dozen researchers produced the report by analyzing data from Canadian ministries of education, though Manitoba and Nunavut did not participate. The researchers examined standardized test results alongside teacher-assigned grades, considering factors such as gender and location, including urban versus rural and remote communities. The report identified a discrepancy between high-stakes standardized tests, which capture a snapshot of knowledge at a specific time, and the grades students receive in class. Vaillancourt noted that grade inflation is a real factor, but clarified this is not a criticism of teachers, who faced high-stress situations during the pandemic. She added that teacher grades often incorporate a student's overall learning progress.

cards.headline: President Mahama provides 111 vehicles and new forensic lab to Ghana's BNI

pages.text: President John Dramani Mahama presented 111 operational vehicles and unveiled a new forensic laboratory and modernized interrogation centre for the Bureau of National Intelligence (BNI) in Accra, Ghana, on November 13, 2026. The BNI is the country's premier intelligence agency. The vehicle fleet includes 100 Mitsubishi pickup trucks, six Toyota Land Cruiser station wagons, and five Toyota Prado vehicles. This equipment is intended to improve the agency's mobility, investigative capacity, and response to contemporary security threats, such as cybercrime and financial fraud. President Mahama noted that a previous lack of vehicles had hampered the Bureau's efficiency, with officers sometimes using old vehicles for intelligence gathering.

The new forensic laboratory is designed to help the BNI probe complex digital offences, including cybercrimes and sophisticated digital fraud. Additionally, the renovated interrogation centre features advanced soundproofing and digital recording equipment. President Mahama stated these upgrades are intended to ensure transparent, accountable, and professional investigative procedures. While charging officers to maintain high standards of vigilance, the President also instructed them to uphold the fundamental rights and dignity of individuals brought in for questioning, noting that the physical environment of the interrogation rooms must balance rigorous state security with strict adherence to human rights.

During the ceremony, President Mahama commended BNI Director-General Charles Alhassan Kipo for his leadership in modernizing the institution. The President noted that the BNI's intelligence supports the police, military, and other agencies. He also mentioned that the BNI's new regional headquarters in the Ahafo Region was recently commissioned, and eight other regional offices are currently being built. The completion of these ongoing projects is expected to bring the number of modernized regional offices to at least nine by 2027. President Mahama announced that additional vehicles would be procured for various security agencies in 2027, with the BNI expected to receive more to expand its fleet.

cards.headline: Stelco recalling 175 laid-off workers at Hamilton steel plant

pages.text: Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers who were laid off earlier this fall. In a news release, the company stated the workers would return to the factory by December and indicated it would retroactively pay them for the time they were laid off. Ron Wells, president of the United Steelworkers Local 1005, called the announcement a “pretty good victory,” telling CBC News Network that the company was forced to live up to its commitments.

The recall follows a September announcement from Cleveland-Cliffs, the American parent company, that it planned to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idled certain steel production at Stelco. Cleveland-Cliffs originally cited competition from imported steel products, weak demand for Canadian steel, and U.S. tariffs as reasons for the planned layoffs. Stelco's statement also cited those issues but noted the company had received reassurances from customers to support its Hamilton finishing operations. The company stated these customers committed to support the operations despite a lack of response from the federal government regarding shortfalls in a tariff-response program and the continued flood of offshore imports of galvanized products.

The federal government has maintained that any move to lay off workers would violate binding commitments made by Cleveland-Cliffs when it bought Stelco in 2024. The government says Cleveland-Cliffs agreed to maintain the number of unionized employees at 2024 levels through 2029 in its original purchase agreement. In mid-October, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to the Ohio-based company demanding it reverse the layoffs or face possible legal action, and she asked the Competition Bureau to investigate the Cleveland-Cliffs purchase of Stelco.

cards.headline: 24-hour vessel operations increase fuel discharge at Tema oil jetty in Ghana

pages.text: Fuel discharge operations at the Tema oil jetty in Ghana have increased following the introduction of round-the-clock berthing and unberthing of vessels. This change, facilitated by the National Petroleum Authority (NPA), allows ships to arrive and depart at any time, addressing a previous limitation where the jetty could not accommodate vessels after 5 p.m. and leaving ships waiting in queues to discharge products, according to NPA Chief Executive Godwin Kudzo Tameklo. On November 12, 2026, during a visit by civil society organizations to offshore mooring facilities, Ghana Petroleum Mooring Systems Company Limited (GPMS) Operations and Maintenance Manager Francis Owusu stated that the improvements have helped increase operational efficiency.

GPMS began the 24-hour operations after resolving technical challenges and upgrading lighting and security arrangements at the facility. The NPA led this process in collaboration with the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority and the Ghana Standards Authority. The multi-purpose oil jetty handles the loading and discharge of several petroleum products, including crude oil, fuel oil, aviation turbine kerosene, gasoil, gasoline, naphtha, and liquefied petroleum gas. The visit to the facilities included the Single Point Mooring (SPM), the oil jetty, and the Conventional Buoy Mooring (CBM). The CBM facility is located approximately 2.7 nautical miles from the Tema Fishing Harbour and uses four permanent mooring chains anchored to the seabed to keep vessels stationary and secured.

Kwadwo Opoku, Executive Director of the Institute for Energy Policy and Research, spoke on behalf of the visiting civil society groups and commended NPA Chief Executive Godwin Kudzo Tameklo for maintaining an open-door policy that provides stakeholders with deeper insight into operations within the downstream petroleum sector.

cards.headline: RCMP release photo of Moncton man charged with child luring and human trafficking

pages.text: Codiac Regional RCMP have released a photo of 45-year-old Timothy Roy, a former realtor in greater Moncton, New Brunswick, who faces several charges following a child luring investigation. Police also released a list of various communities across Canada where Roy has “spent time in” since 2000, including locations in Ontario, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and Labrador. Investigators are encouraging anyone who may have had interactions with Roy or believes they may have been victimized to contact the RCMP or local police in their area.

The investigation began on Aug. 26 after police received information that a 45-year-old man was in contact with underage girls for a sexual purpose. On the evening of Sept. 10, officers located a vehicle belonging to the suspect parked at a hotel on Mountain Road in Moncton. The following day, the man was seen exiting the hotel with a female under the age of 16 and was arrested at the scene, according to RCMP spokesperson Cpl. Luc Picard. Roy was charged in Moncton provincial court on Sept. 15 and remains in custody pending a future court appearance. He faces charges of sexual assault, sexual interference of a person under the age of 16, human trafficking of a person under 18, child luring, and obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under 18.

cards.headline: Approximately 200 unarmed police officers deployed to Nalerigu, Ghana, for NDC regional election

pages.text: About 200 unarmed police officers arrived at Nalerigu Senior High School on Saturday, November 14, 2026, to provide security for the National Democratic Congress (NDC) regional executive election. The police stated the deployment is intended to guarantee a free, fair, and orderly election involving a total of 231 delegates. While the officers on-site are unarmed, the police disclosed that armed personnel have been placed on standby to respond to any eventuality that might threaten security during the exercise. A commander urged candidates, supporters, and party stakeholders to conduct themselves responsibly to avoid undermining the electoral process.

The security presence follows deepening divisions within the NDC in the Nalerigu-Gambaga Constituency, which have led to legal disputes and public exchanges between rival party executives. These disagreements involve the selection and legitimacy of five co-opted constituency executives and whether they are eligible to participate in the regional election. Consequently, an application to the Nalerigu High Court resulted in a restraint preventing five individuals from participating in the election. Internal tensions have also surfaced a political rivalry between Regional Minister Ibrahim Tia and Alhaji Baba Issifu, a former Nalerigu-Gambaga MP and former Minister for Climate Change, regarding political influence in the constituency.

cards.headline: Village inside Karnataka's Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary lacks roads, schools, and hospitals

pages.text: Residents of Paradeshappana Mutt, a village located near Sirivase in Chikkamagaluru taluk, live without roads, public transport, schools, hospitals, or electricity supply from utility companies. Situated deep inside the Bhadra Wildlife Sanctuary in Karnataka, the village is home to approximately 30 families. The majority of these residents belong to the Adi Karnataka, a Scheduled Caste, though a couple of residents do not. The village is named after a mutt that has existed there for centuries.

The lack of infrastructure forces residents to travel on foot or by personal two-wheeler to the nearest village, Bogase, even for basic essentials like salt. While houses have recently been lit at night using solar panels donated by private companies, Rudraiah, a resident in his 70s, and his cousin Kalaiah stated they had never seen a lightbulb in their homes before. Due to the absence of local schools, families send their children to stay with relatives or in hostels in distant locations for their studies.

cards.headline: Burning plastic waste in East Java village linked to respiratory disease concerns

pages.text: In Sumberejo, a village in East Java, Indonesia, residents have historically burned plastic waste in limestone kilns to produce building materials. While this practice supported local livelihoods, the resulting smoke may have a devastating impact on health. Ahmad Yani, a resident from Brawijaya University, reported that some individuals he knew who operated the limestone kilns died from respiratory diseases, though the causes were never determined. Mr. Yani stated that the burning of plastics in his village is no longer happening.

cards.headline: Dozens of Afghans in US experience relief as deportation plans appear paused

pages.text: Dozens of Afghans currently in the United States are experiencing what Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, described as “fragile relief” after it appeared the Trump administration put on hold plans to remove them within days. The group, which includes individuals who fear being killed by the Taliban if returned to Afghanistan, faced potential deportation following the expiration of a temporary court order that had previously blocked a flight scheduled for election day. The New York Times reported that the total group numbers more than 150 Afghans. The Associated Press previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.

On November 10, 2026, it was learned that at least one Afghan man in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government. This development followed concerns from immigration advocates that detainees could have been forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November. Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they might not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days. Members of Congress and advocates have warned that these deportations could effectively be a death sentence for those being returned.

cards.headline: Researchers find fossilized evidence of blood in 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone

pages.text: Researchers have discovered fossilized evidence of blood inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur leg bone. A team led by Kliti Grice, a geochemist from Curtin University in Australia, found molecular evidence of heme—an iron-rich molecule found in blood—inside the bone. This discovery, published in the journal PNAS, includes the identification of microscopic structures that resemble red blood cells and other chemical fingerprints of blood. The findings suggest that certain biomolecules can persist much longer than previously thought when preserved under special burial conditions.

cards.headline: Archaeological discoveries in Saudi Arabia reveal human activity dating back around 125,000 years

pages.text: Archaeological discoveries at the Uruq Al-Julaybah site in Najran, Saudi Arabia, have revealed evidence of human activity dating back around 125,000 years. The findings, published in the journal Science, indicate that the area was once part of a lush environment featuring freshwater lakes and grasslands during a humid period of the Arabian Peninsula's history. This site was located on the shores of the Mundafan paleolake, a former body of water that researchers suggest covered approximately 340 square kilometers and reached depths of nearly 29 meters. These conditions provided a stable freshwater environment and abundant wildlife that supported early human settlement in what is now part of the Empty Quarter.

The multidisciplinary study was conducted by the Kingdom’s Heritage Commission in collaboration with King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Australia’s Griffith University, and several other Saudi and international research institutions. Researchers documented more than 130 archaeological locations and recorded more than 500 fossils of plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates. These fossils included hippopotamuses, extinct long-horned buffalo, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, ostriches, mollusks, and freshwater crustaceans. The team also recovered 5,511 stone artifacts, with more than 98 percent made from flint. Analysis showed these tools were created using the Levallois technique, an advanced stone-tool manufacturing method that requires precision and planning to control the specific shape and size of flakes and points.

Microscopic and chemical examinations of the artifacts identified preserved traces of wood, resins, fats, collagen, and plant fibers, suggesting daily activities involving both animal and plant resources. Some stone points showed evidence of hafting—the process of attaching a tool to a handle—as well as impact fractures. While researchers detected compounds from Acokanthera schimperi, a plant historically linked to hunting, the study noted there was insufficient evidence to determine exactly how the material was used. Abdullah Alsharekh of King Saud University stated the Mundafan shores provided an ideal habitat by combining freshwater, vegetation, and raw materials for survival. Professor Michael Petraglia of Griffith University said the discovery advances the understanding of early human settlement in the region, while KAUST geology professor Dr. Frans van Buchem noted the effort helped create a more complete picture of ancient human behavior.

cards.headline: Inactivating part of a patient's right amygdala reduced PTSD symptoms and threat perception

pages.text: A case study published in Nature Communications involving a man with drug-resistant epilepsy and severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) suggests that activity in the right amygdala may help sustain PTSD symptoms. During an awake bedside procedure, researchers selectively inactivated part of the man's right amygdala, which reduced his tendency to perceive ambiguous faces as fearful and was followed by a sharp drop in his trauma symptoms. While the findings are drawn from a single patient, they offer unusual causal evidence regarding how the amygdala contributes to threat-focused biases and PTSD symptoms. Standard brain imaging typically only captures correlations, leaving it uncertain whether abnormal amygdala activity drives negative interpretation bias or merely accompanies it. Studying targeted neurosurgery offers a rare way to observe the effects of directly disrupting amygdala function.

PTSD is a psychiatric condition that can develop after severe trauma, characterized by intrusive memories, avoidance of trauma reminders, negative shifts in mood and thinking, and persistent physical jumpiness. A central feature of the disorder is negative interpretation bias, which is the tendency to read neutral or ambiguous cues, such as an unreadable facial expression, as threatening. This bias can cause individuals to see everyday surroundings as dangerous, keeping fear responses active and making emotions harder to regulate. The amygdala—a pair of almond-shaped neuron clusters located deep inside the brain’s left and right temporal lobes, roughly behind the temples—helps detect danger and coordinate fear responses. Brain scans consistently show heightened amygdala reactivity to fearful or neutral sights in people with PTSD.

cards.headline: Forensic examination of 5,000-year-old skulls suggests human sacrifice in ancient Egypt

pages.text: A modern forensic examination of 46 skulls recovered near royal tombs in Abydos, Egypt, has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of the remains. This finding, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied, provides new evidence suggesting that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed upon their deaths, possibly to allow those individuals to continue serving them in the afterlife. The skulls belonged to members of the First Dynasty, who were buried roughly 5,000 years ago near the earliest kings of a unified Egypt. The research was led by Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University and published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The discovery provides physical evidence for a burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he observed that unusually large numbers of people were buried around the kings. While Petrie suspected these individuals had been sacrificed following the deaths of their rulers, he was unable to identify physical evidence of fatal injuries at that time. Dr. Campbell, who is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press), noted that these retainers are often relegated to footnotes in the broader historical narrative and raised questions regarding how these individuals viewed the ruler and their own roles in the ruler's life and death.

cards.headline: Large Asian elephant herds in Sri Lanka fracture into smaller, less resilient groups after member losses

pages.text: Large herds of Asian elephants in Sri Lanka reach a tipping point where they fracture into smaller, isolated groups following losses from poaching, old age, disease, or drought. These smaller groups are more susceptible to further losses from the same external threats, reducing the overall resilience of the population. Unlike African elephants, which live in unrelated bachelor herds and related matriarch-led families, Asian elephant society is more fluid, with unrelated members frequently joining or leaving groups. In both species, offspring generally benefit from the protection and care provided by a larger number of adults. Researchers tracking 443 female elephants over 12 years initially identified 20 groups with an average of 14 members each.

The study, published in the journal Science, was led by University of California, San Diego Assistant Professor Shermin de Silva. Behavioral ecologist Anastasia Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Cincinnati, analyzed the data on wild elephants in Sri Lanka for the University of California, San Diego as part of a long-term demographic project. The research notes that elephants in Sri Lanka live in suboptimal habitats increasingly dominated by an inedible invasive species and live near human populations, leading to frequent deadly conflicts for both elephants and people.

cards.headline: Touch-based brain interface enables control of extra robotic arms during manual tasks

pages.text: Researchers have developed a touch-based brain-computer interface that allows people to command extra robotic arms while simultaneously using their own hands without disrupting natural physical coordination, according to a study published in Nature Communications by Jia et al. (2026). A brain-computer interface is a system that measures electrical activity in the brain, often through small sensors resting against the scalp, and translates specific signal patterns into commands for external machines. While much research in this field focuses on restoring movement for those with paralysis or injury, this work explores movement augmentation, which involves equipping able-bodied individuals with extra robotic limbs or fingers to perform tasks beyond the capacity of two biological hands. Tianyu Jia, a postdoctoral researcher in bioengineering at Imperial College London, noted that the initial inspiration for the project came partly from the fictional Spider-Man character Doctor Octopus.

In the study, volunteers used the interface to select among four distinct robotic commands. To do this, four small vibrators were strapped to the upper and lower arms, each buzzing in short bursts in a random order. Each vibrator represented a different command; by focusing attention on a specific vibration, participants triggered a brainwave response that the system decoded to move the robotic arms. To test if this could be done while multitasking, participants performed a manual ball-balancing task using a clear tray. After three days of practice, the accuracy gap between participants moving both their hands and those sitting still was no longer statistically significant.

cards.headline: Evolution may have altered instructions for producing brain-building cells

pages.text: Researchers in Taiwan and Japan have identified a small region of DNA that helps control the production of specialized neural stem cells, suggesting that evolution can create new developmental possibilities without necessarily creating entirely new genes. This finding, published in the journal Science Advances, provides a new perspective on how the primate brain achieves its size and complexity compared to other mammals. While previous discoveries showed how genetic changes can increase the number of brain cells or extend how long those cells multiply, this research indicates that evolution may also alter the instructions that determine which specific types of brain-building cells are produced.

The study was led by researchers at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and Academia Sinica, with collaborators from Kyoto University. To understand the mechanism, the researchers compared the process to a factory where neural stem cells act as workers that produce the cells making up the brain. In this model, evolution can change the brain by expanding the workforce, extending production hours, or changing the operating instructions to produce a different mix of workers. This discovery identifies the latter mechanism: a change in the instructions used to produce specific types of cells.

cards.headline: Yale scientists identify treatments that influence biological aging

pages.text: Scientists at Yale have identified that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests, while popular over-the-counter supplements showed little evidence of producing similar effects. The findings, published in Nature Medicine, aim to help researchers more effectively evaluate anti-aging treatments by distinguishing between those that influence biological aging and those that show little measurable benefit. However, researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean individuals will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

The research was conducted by Raghav Sehgal, an associate research scientist in psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. Sehgal, who previously planned to use computer science techniques to investigate cancer, shifted his research focus toward the underlying aging process that contributes to the development of diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. He noted that researchers still have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and determining if management steps are truly effective.
